title: Market Pulse: AI Infrastructure Selloff Broadens Into Market-Wide Deleveraging
summary: Verification pending: Thursday's semiconductor rout spread across all S&P 500 sectors, reversing post-election relief; Treasury yields declined even as oil rebounded and the Bank of England raised rates.
reviewed_by: BLAQUE BAUX automated research desk; independent editorial verification pending

sections.heading: What Happened: Observed
paragraphs: Thursday's selloff overturned the morning's relatively narrow futures divergence. Reuters reported at 12:24 p.m. ET that the Dow was down 2.63%, the S&P 500 3.41% and Nasdaq Composite 4.55%; all eleven S&P 500 sectors were negative. These are intraday snapshots, not closing prices. Source: Reuters, November 5.

By StockTitan's 2:01 p.m. ET snapshot, Nvidia was down 8.62% and AMD 15.40%; its 2:13 p.m. ET update described continued semiconductor-led selling. The Nasdaq was approaching a correction from its prior peak. Source: StockTitan, November 5.

Reuters reported Brent around $97 per barrel, up 2.58%, and the U.S. 10-year Treasury yield near 4.88% during the global selloff. Oil's rebound complicates Wednesday's energy-disinflation narrative. The Bank of England raised its policy rate to 4%, citing inflation pressures. Source: Reuters global markets, November 5.

Initial U.S. unemployment claims declined 6,000 to 189,000; continuing claims rose 23,000 to 1.718 million. Third-quarter productivity strengthened and unit labor costs declined, offering a counterpoint to inflation fears. Source: Reuters, November 5.
A synchronized, verified cash VIX level and investment-grade/high-yield spread snapshot were not established; no figures are inferred.

sections.heading: What Mattered: Interpretation
paragraphs: The change since the morning pulse is decisive: weakness moved from technology-specific futures into a broad cash-equity drawdown. Falling Treasury yields alongside sharply lower stocks indicate demand for safer duration, not necessarily easier financing for AI-linked borrowers.

Concerns about permitting and restrictions on new data centers are interacting with existing questions about AI capital expenditure and customer cash returns. A delayed project can affect power suppliers, accelerator orders, server integrators, construction contractors, equipment lessors and lenders at different times; the magnitude of those effects remains unverified.

Resilient jobless claims and lower unit labor costs complicate a simple recession or inflation narrative. The energy rebound and Bank of England tightening demonstrate that policy risks are not uniformly easing.

sections.heading: What We're Watching
list: Friday's U.S. October employment report: payrolls, unemployment, wages and Treasury repricing.
Market breadth and cash volatility into the close; determine whether selling is indiscriminate or concentrated in leveraged AI exposure.
Corporate credit confirmation: AI issuer CDS, financing terms and broad investment-grade/high-yield spreads; do not assume contagion without spread evidence.
Data-center policy proposals, permitting timelines, power availability and any concrete changes to signed supplier or customer commitments.
Brent, Hormuz tanker traffic and insurance pricing; distinguish physical supply recovery from diplomatic headlines.

sections.heading: Where We See Things Going
paragraphs: If credit spreads remain contained and policymakers clarify the scope of data-center restrictions, a partial technical rebound is plausible following the sharp repricing. This would not by itself establish improved cash returns.

If selling begins to raise funding costs or delay projects while energy prices rebound, broader capital-expenditure retrenchment becomes more likely. No numerical probabilities or index targets are justified by the available intraday evidence.
